claims.text: A uniform, thin Ni interlayer can be deposited conformally on W surfaces before W–Cu composite assembly.
A Ni interlayer on W surfaces will mitigate phase separation in a W–Cu composite.
A Ni interlayer will suppress W–Cu interfacial void formation under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
Suppressing interfacial void formation with a Ni interlayer will enhance thermal conductivity relative to an untreated W–Cu composite.
The proposed composite consists of W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix.
The engineered Ni interlayer will improve bonding at the W–Cu interface.
The engineered Ni interlayer will reduce local interfacial-energy mismatches at the W–Cu interface.
The Ni coating acts as a diffusion barrier at the W–Cu interface.
The Ni coating promotes wetting at the W–Cu interface.
The Ni coating reduces the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation.
Reduced phase separation minimizes interfacial void nucleation.
Reduced void nucleation preserves a more coherent W–Cu interface under thermal and irradiation stresses.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will retain a more stable microstructure than untreated composites under comparable service conditions.
Untreated W–Cu composites tend to undergo phase separation during heat transfer and irradiation.
Untreated W–Cu composites tend to form interfacial voids during heat transfer and irradiation.
Phase separation and interfacial void formation degrade the thermal performance of untreated W–Cu composites.
Nonuniform Ni coating thickness may limit the effectiveness of the interlayer.
Extreme temperatures or prolonged irradiation may cause Ni diffusion that limits interlayer effectiveness.
